The Education

Why OB-GYN Billing Is the Most Documentation-Intensive Specialty in Medicine

The global OB package bundles months of care into a single claim then unbundles exceptions that most practices never capture. PMEx manages both simultaneously.

OB-GYN billing covers two fundamentally different clinical environments obstetrics, governed by the global OB package concept, and gynecology, governed by surgical coding with its own set of modifiers, global periods, and fee schedule rules. Each requires distinct billing expertise, and most OB-GYN practices manage both simultaneously.

The global OB package bundles up to 13 antepartum visits (vaginal delivery) or 12 (cesarean), the delivery itself, and postpartum care into a single bundled payment. The package works when the same physician or group provides all care. It requires unbundling when: the patient changes providers mid-pregnancy, Medicaid requires per-visit billing, the patient delivers early, or high-risk complications generate separately billable services outside the routine package. High-risk pregnancy complications pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes requiring insulin, preterm labor management are not included in the global package and must be billed separately to capture their full clinical value.

Gynecologic surgery billing involves high-value procedures laparoscopic hysterectomy, myomectomy, complex pelvic reconstruction with surgical assistant billing, bilateral modifier applications, and multiple procedure reduction rules. A missed surgical assistant code on a total laparoscopic hysterectomy costs $200 to $800 per case. Bilateral oophorectomy coded as unilateral loses $150 to $300 per surgery.

Medicaid maternity billing adds a third layer. Every state's Medicaid program has specific rules for global period billing, antepartum visit count thresholds, and enhanced reimbursement for high-risk services. Billing Medicaid maternity incorrectly creates both revenue loss and potential recoupment exposure the Pennsylvania case study below shows $95K in recoupment demand resolved.

The unbundling opportunity most OB practices miss:

High-risk pregnancy antepartum visits that generate separately billable services (pre-eclampsia management, IUGR monitoring, threatened preterm labor) should be unbundled from the global package. Each unbundled episode recovers $800 to $2,200 per high-risk delivery case for care the physician is already providing.

The Revenue OB Practices Systematically Miss

The Global OB Package Unbundling Gap

The global OB package (59400 for vaginal delivery, 59510 for cesarean) bundles routine antepartum care, the delivery, and postpartum care into a single payment. The word "routine" is the billing key. When a pregnancy develops complications that require separately billable services not included in the routine package, those services must be unbundled and billed individually but only when correct documentation supports the unbundling.

Pre-eclampsia management visits, IUGR monitoring with biophysical profiles, threatened preterm labor management, and gestational diabetes requiring insulin with multiple monitoring visits each of these generates clinical work that is NOT included in the global OB package and CAN be billed separately with the correct diagnosis and procedure codes. Most OB practices include all of these visits in the global package and forgo the additional revenue entirely.

PMEx tracks every pregnant patient's pregnancy complication status and flags visits that qualify for unbundling from the global package. High-risk antepartum visits are billed separately with correct E/M codes, diagnostic procedure codes, and the diagnosis codes supporting the medical complexity. Routine visits continue within the global package. The practice captures both.

Global Package Error

High-Risk Visits Incorrectly Bundled

Pre-eclampsia monitoring visits, IUGR biophysical profiles, and preterm labor management visits included in global package. These services are separately billable outside the routine global each visit forfeited costs $200 to $600 in unbillable revenue.

PMEx monitors every patient's active diagnoses for unbundling triggers. High-risk complication visits are flagged and billed separately with correct E/M and procedure codes before submission.

Delivery Code Error

VBAC Coded as Standard Vaginal Delivery

VBAC (vaginal birth after cesarean) billed using standard vaginal delivery codes (59400) instead of VBAC-specific codes (59610 global, 59614 delivery only). Some payers require prior authorization for VBAC delivery authorization not obtained. Double billing error: wrong code and missing auth.

PMEx reviews prior cesarean history for every patient before delivery codes are selected. VBAC codes applied from patient history documentation. VBAC-specific prior authorizations obtained from payers that require them before delivery.

Medicaid Maternity Error

State Medicaid Global Package Rules Violated

Medicaid maternity billing submitted using global package codes when the state program requires per-visit billing. Or per-visit billing submitted when Medicaid requires global billing. Either direction triggers recoupment demand from state Medicaid as in the $95K New York case.

PMEx maintains per-state Medicaid maternity billing rules and routes every Medicaid patient to the correct billing method global package or per-visit based on the patient's state and plan. Zero Medicaid maternity billing method errors.

Fertility Auth Gap

IVF Cycle Initiated Without Authorization

REI practice proceeds with IVF cycle start before authorization confirmed. Payer reviews and denies cycle costs retroactively drug administration, egg retrieval (58970), and embryo transfer (58974) denied. $8,000 to $15,000 in cycle costs unrecoverable after the fact.

PMEx Prior Auth obtains IVF cycle authorization before any cycle protocol begins submitting with infertility diagnosis documentation, prior treatment history, and cycle count. Authorization confirmed in writing before egg retrieval is scheduled.

Surgical Modifier Error

GYN Surgery Missing Bilateral or Assistant Modifier

Bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy coded as unilateral procedure. Modifier 50 not applied. Payer reimburses 100% instead of 150% for bilateral. Or surgical assistant participating in laparoscopic hysterectomy assistant billing never submitted. $200 to $800 per case systematically forfeited.

PMEx reviews every operative report for bilateral procedures and surgical assistant documentation before coding. Modifier 50 or RT/LT applied correctly per payer. Surgical assistant billing submitted as a separate professional claim where documentation supports it.

Postpartum Unbundle

Postpartum Complications Not Separately Billed

Postpartum hemorrhage requiring additional intervention, postpartum infection requiring IV antibiotics, or postpartum depression management visit all occurring after the global package delivery billed within the global package rather than separately. Each is a separately billable service not included in the routine postpartum component.

PMEx monitors discharge and postpartum visit documentation for complications occurring after delivery. Postpartum complications are billed separately from the global package postpartum visit. Revenue captured for clinical work that exceeds the routine postpartum component.

OB-GYN Billing Answered

PMEx tracks global OB package components for every pregnant patient antepartum visit counts, delivery type, and postpartum care and submits the complete global package (59400, 59510) or individual components (59425/59426 antepartum, 59409/59514 delivery only, 59430 postpartum) based on what the physician actually provided. We track mid-trimester provider changes and unbundle correctly when required by payer or Medicaid rules.

Unbundling is required when: a provider change occurs mid-pregnancy, the patient delivers before the typical visit count threshold, Medicaid requires per-visit billing, or high-risk complications (pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, IUGR, preterm labor) generate separately billable services not included in the global package. PMEx tracks these situations automatically and codes each component correctly recovering $800 to $2,200 per high-risk delivery case.
